nameStory: The 'waxwing' name comes from the bright red, waxy-looking tips on some of their wing feathers that really do resemble drops of red sealing wax. 'Bohemian' refers to their nomadic lifestyle - like the wandering peoples once called Bohemians, these birds roam unpredictably across the landscape in search of fruit. Some winters they stay up north, other years they suddenly appear in huge flocks far south of their usual range.
description: The Bohemian Waxwing is a sleek, starling-sized bird with silky smooth plumage in soft buff-gray tones. These social birds sport a distinctive pointed crest on their heads and dramatic black face markings that look like a bandit's mask. Their wings flash with bright yellow and white patterns, and if you look closely, some wing feathers have those famous red waxy tips. They're slightly larger and more robust-looking than their Cedar Waxwing cousins.

idTips.label: Pointed Crest
idTips.description: A sharp, triangular crest that can be raised or lowered, giving the head a distinctive pointed silhouette even when relaxed

idTips.label: Black Face Mask
idTips.description: Bold black markings across the eyes and face create a striking bandit-mask appearance against the buff-colored head

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Wings show bright yellow bands and white markings that flash dramatically in flight, plus those telltale red waxy wing tips on some feathers

idTips.label: Silky Plumage
idTips.description: Overall feathers have an unusually smooth, almost velvety texture that gives the bird a refined, polished appearance

idTips.label: Social Flocking
idTips.description: Almost always seen in groups, often large flocks that move and feed together with synchronized movements

idTips.label: Fruit-Eating Behavior
idTips.description: Watch for birds methodically stripping berries from trees and bushes, often hanging upside down to reach fruit

habitat: In New England, look for Bohemian Waxwings in areas with abundant fruit-bearing trees and shrubs, especially during winter irruptions. They favor mountain ash (rowan) trees, crabapples, and ornamental fruit trees in towns and suburbs. During their unpredictable winter visits, they're often found in parks, residential areas with berry-producing landscaping, and forest edges near water sources.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England during spring as most birds have returned to northern breeding grounds. Any lingering individuals would still be in flocks seeking remaining winter fruits.
seasonality.summer: Not typically present in New England during breeding season, as they nest much farther north in boreal forests. Summer sightings would be exceptional.
seasonality.fall: First arrivals possible in late fall during irruption years, when flocks begin moving south in search of fruit. Look for early flocks in areas with abundant berry crops.
seasonality.winter: Peak time for New England sightings during irruption years, when large flocks arrive to feed on mountain ash berries, crabapples, and other persistent fruits. Can be remarkably tame and approachable.

funFact: Bohemian Waxwings can actually get drunk from eating fermented berries, sometimes to the point where they become dangerously intoxicated and unable to fly properly - they've even been found passed out under fruit trees after particularly wild berry binges!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the smaller Cedar Waxwing, but Bohemians are noticeably larger with more prominent white wing markings and rusty-colored undertail coverts (the area under the tail). Memory trick: Bohemians are the 'bigger, bolder' waxwing with more dramatic wing patterns.
contextualKnowledge: Bohemian Waxwings are classic 'irruptive' species - they don't migrate on a predictable schedule but instead stage dramatic population movements called irruptions when food runs short in the north. Some winters New England sees none at all, while other years thousands suddenly appear, creating exciting birding opportunities.
compareHints: Bohemian Waxwings are significantly larger than Cedar Waxwings and have much more striking wing patterns with prominent white markings. While Cedar Waxwings have yellow tail bands, Bohemians show rusty-colored undertail coverts and generally appear more robust overall. Bohemians also travel in larger, more dramatic flocks during their irregular winter irruptions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cedar Waxwings are smaller and browner than their rare relative the Bohemian Waxwing, which is grayer overall and has rusty-red under the tail.
